content.content:
## 5. The answer

Nothing in `FortressLibrary.fss` is written for the interpreter's *evaluation*
strategy. 95.3% of it is plain Fortress that the bytecode compiler would be
happy to compile. What is specific to bytecode generation is the 4.7% of native
bindings — and even those are mostly already ported, on the Java side, in
`nativeHelpers/`.

What breaks, and when:

1. **Nothing at DISAMBIGUATE**, once `FortressLibrary` is the prelude rather
   than a component competing with `CompilerBuiltin`. (Compiled as an ordinary
   component it produces 1,417 disambiguation errors, 78% of them the two
   preludes colliding — a red herring.)
2. **92 errors at TYPECHECK**, in the library's *apis*, before the component is
   opened: 62 of them the `comprises`/exclusion rules rejecting the numeric and
   comparison tower (`TotalComparison`, `QQ`, `AnyIntegral`, `Integral[\I\]`,
   `ZZ`/`ZZ32`/`ZZ64`/`NN64`, `AnyMaybe`), 26 of them `Integral[\I\]` bounds
   that the range library does not satisfy. The 2012 team never saw these
   because `walk` sets `fortress.compile.typecheck` false and `StaticChecker`
   returns the tree untouched.
3. **A hard crash at TYPECHECK**, `java.lang.Error: Not yet implemented`,
   whenever a `nat`-kinded static parameter has to be inferred — and a
   different crash (`ClassCastException: VarType cannot be cast to IntExpr`)
   when one is given explicitly. Reproduced in six lines with the compiler's
   own prelude. 81 declarations in `FortressLibrary.fss` and 58 in its api
   carry such a parameter; `CompilerBuiltin.fss` carries none and
   `CompilerLibrary.fss` carries one, declared empty.
4. **DESUGAR and CODEGEN: untested.** Nothing got that far.

Therefore "use `FortressLibrary` for the compiler too" is **not** a port of 108
native bindings plus a handful of checker complaints. It is three things, in
this order:

* implement `nat`/`int` static parameters in the Scala type checker
  (`STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` and the `StaticTypeReplacer` path behind
  `pNat2`) — or rewrite the library to avoid them, which means giving up
  `Vector[\T,nat s\]`, `Matrix[\T,nat r,nat c\]` and `Array1..3`, i.e. the
  array vocabulary the whole exercise wants;
* fix, or relax, 92 type errors in a hierarchy that has never been checked —
  a language-design conversation about `comprises` and exclusion, not a typo
  hunt;
* then port the 108 native bindings, ~79 of which already have a Java
  counterpart in `nativeHelpers/`.

And only then would we learn what DESUGAR and CODEGEN make of it.


# Can the compiler just use `FortressLibrary`?

Pavol's question, verbatim:

> I still don't get why the library needs to be rewritten for the compiler,
> other than your guess that the interpreter's standard library would not pass
> the type checker. What's specific to bytecode generation in there? Couldn't
> the path forward be just to use the FortressLibrary for the compiler as
> well? What breaks and when?

Answered by trying it. Every command and its full output is in this directory;
`run-all.sh` lists them in order. Host: JDK 25.0.3, `source experiment/env.sh`
(`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`), tree at HEAD, caches wiped and the
compiler library chain rebuilt from scratch first (106 s, `01-library-chain.out`).
Nothing outside this directory was modified.

**The short answer.** Almost nothing in `FortressLibrary.fss` is about bytecode
generation. 4.7% of it (211 of 4,518 lines) is native bindings, and those are
the *only* genuinely codegen-specific thing in the file. What actually stops
"use FortressLibrary for the compiler too" is not codegen at all: it is that
`compile` turns the type checker **on** and `walk` leaves it **off**, and the
interpreter's library has never been through the type checker. When you make
`FortressLibrary` the compiler's prelude, disambiguation passes with **zero**
errors, and then the type checker reports **92 errors** in the library's own
apis and **crashes outright** — `java.lang.Error: Not yet implemented` — on the
`nat`-kinded static parameters the library is built out of. Desugar and codegen
are never reached, in any run, by any variant. So the port is not 108 native
bindings plus a few checker fixes: it is (a) 108 native bindings, (b) a library
type hierarchy that violates the exclusion rules the checker enforces, and
(c) an unimplemented piece of the type checker itself.

homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

The question is about what your "one library" decision actually decided.

**What the two libraries are.** The interpreter has the full standard library, 4.5K lines, the one every microGPT program runs on. The compiler has its own small prelude, written 2008 as a "stripped-down minimalist library for first crack at compilation", a "hopefully temporary hack" in the team's words. On 2026-09-20 you decided the prelude is a bootstrap to get rid of: the interpreter's library becomes the one library the compiler checks, and the prelude's three files are deleted at the switch-over.

**Where the two differ on numbers.** In the interpreter's library the numbers nest: a `ZZ32` is a `ZZ64`, which is a `ZZ` (unbounded integer), which is a `QQ` (rational), which is an `RR64` (double), which is a `Number`. That is the mathematical picture, ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ, and it is why `Number`'s catch-all operations serve every level and microGPT can mix integers and floats freely. In the compiler's prelude Steele flattened this in July 2011: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and the rest sit side by side under `Number`, none a subtype of another, and a narrower value is widened by a declared `coerce` that the compiler inserts where needed. Every language you named as a peer (Java, Swift, Rust, Julia, X10) has the flat shape.

**Why it matters for the checker.** Each level of the nested tower declares "I am `Equality` at my own type", so one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five different instantiations at once. The exclusion rule forbids exactly that, and it is 61 of the checker's 103 errors on the library. In the flat shape every type is `Equality` at one instantiation, the errors vanish, and the checker is not touched. That is route A: keep the rule, give the one library's tower the prelude's shape. The other two routes keep the nesting and change the checker instead.

**The reading that would rule A out.** The judge who examined rung P's finding struck A on this ground: you chose the interpreter's library, and A would reshape its tower into the prelude's, which he read as re-importing the prelude's design after deleting its files. Two of your own statements lean that way: "the library's own practice is the standard" (09-19), and your row 330 reasoning "ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower". The brief's counter-reading: the decision as recorded settled which files survive, not that every design choice inside them is frozen.

**So the question is:** when you said "one library, the interpreter's", did you mean only the files, or also its nested numeric tower? If the tower is part of what you chose, A is out. Then B drops the specialisation shortcut, which you called a must, so C is what remains: the patents' forest rule, where the soundness rule is ours to derive, 40 to 70 lines with no source. In practice the question is "flatten the numbers, as the team did for the compiled world" against "build the type theory they sketched and never built".

Recorded in POSITIONS as reactions, not decisions (`b49f6a4ef`). Answers per question:

**1, coercion.** Today a `ZZ32` value *is* an `RR64`, so `Number`'s catch-all `+` takes both. Under coercion they are separate types, and the library declares a conversion, `RR64 coerce(z: ZZ32)`, which the compiler inserts wherever an `RR64` is expected and no declaration applies without it. That is the spec's own mechanism between `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, and the compiler prelude already runs on 15 such lines. What you keep: `x: RR64 = someInteger` works, mixed arithmetic works, row 330's decision stands with "promotion" restated as "coercion". What you give up: ℤ as a subtype of ℚ in the type relation itself, and `Empty extends List[\T\]`. The one known open item: generic code over mixed widths, where the join of a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` becomes a trait without arithmetic; the brief lists it as unsettled.

**2, the forest rule and POPL 2019.** A correction: the published path did not continue the forest route. POPL 2019 keeps the rule for invariant traits, allows two instantiations only when a single minimal ancestor exists (a cousin of the forest rule, for covariant traits), keeps specialisation by checking the return type at run time (the option Naden rejected), and has no self types and no numeric tower. So on the tower, the group's last published word is "rule kept, no nesting", which is A's shape. The forest rule survives only in the patents, filed on the last day and never built. Your "yes" stands as your weighting; the fact underneath it is narrower than you read it.

**3, which files survive.** Recorded. Route A stays on the table.

**4, the specialisation shortcut.** Two things get called specialisation. One: the class loader stamps out a class per type argument, like C++ templates. Every route keeps that, and unboxing will build on it. Two: a hand-written special version of a generic function for one instantiation under the same name, `dot(v: Vector[\RR64\])` beside `dot[\T\](v: Vector[\T\])`, picked at run time by the value's type. That is the shortcut; the exclusion rule exists to make it sound; B forbids it. Your "as long as it runs fast" is an answer: keep it unless someone shows fast without it, and nobody has. So B is out on your own terms, which the brief also concluded.

**5, run-time coercion in the interpreter.** The spec says the checker decides at compile time where a coercion goes; the compiled path does that already. The interpreter has no checker, so it can only find out at run time, at dispatch: when no overload matches, try the declared coercions. Same program, same answer in the normal case, the choice made later; that is the divergence. Not the class loader (that is the compiled path's). JIT: not relevant here, the interpreter is our oracle, not the target, and its speed is irrelevant by your rule. On the compiled path a coercion is a static call to a small function, inlined by the JIT, costing the boxing every operation pays today until unboxing lands. Can it run first: yes, that is A's first rung, 150 to 200 lines in six interpreter files, no library line changed, the gate green throughout because today's tower needs no coercion.

## 4. The decision

What we do: make the specification's default library, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, the compiler's prelude, and delete `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra` when the switch-over lands; from now on no declaration goes into the compiler prelude, and codegen rungs continue.

What it changes: the standard library exists once; every library edit is gated by both suites; the checker becomes usable on interpreter programs when the prelude passes it; the array vocabulary is not written a second time; the thirteen revival commits to the compiler prelude are superseded and their tests kept.

The documents exist. Two of them, in this order:

1. **The territory map**, `explorations/coordinator/map/README.md`, written on the sixteenth at your request, with its part two `map/modules-and-phases.md`: both pipelines phase by phase, the cache, the runtime, the native interop, and the one table where the two paths diverge.

For `nat` specifically there is `explorations/reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`, the plan that was written and never reviewed, and today's array review judged it.

Your mental model is right up to the class loader, so here is that last piece in plain words. Parsing gives the syntax tree. Names are resolved. On the compile path the checker, in Scala, walks the tree, works out a type for every expression and writes it onto the tree, refusing what breaks the rules. Desugaring rewrites some constructs into simpler ones. The code generator walks the typed tree and writes class files into a cache. Then `fortress run` starts a second JVM with that cache on its class path. The class loader's trick is for generics: a generic trait is compiled once, to a template class with placeholders for its type parameters, and the first time the program needs a specific instance, say a box of doubles, the loader takes the template's bytecode and rewrites it on the spot to that instance. No compiler runs at run time; it is a search-and-replace over bytecode, done by the same bytecode library the compiler uses. Sizes are the open question there: today the loader stamps type names and nothing else, and a size in a type dies at load time with a missing class.

What "teaching the checker `nat`" entails, at the level you need: the checker represents every static argument as a type. A size is not a type, so three things do not exist: a representation for a size, the rule for when two sizes are equal, and inference of a size from a value's shape. Today any two sizes compare equal, so nothing is checked. The theory is old and known, not research: index types with natural-number constraints, Xi and Pfenning's Dependent ML from 1999, and its descendants in Haskell's type-level naturals and X10's constrained types, X10 being Fortress's sibling in the same DARPA programme. The work is implementation in the Scala checker, and the plan already names the files.

The map does not have a page written for exactly this reading, so an Opus worker is writing one now: the compile path from source to running bytecode, one page per stage, what the checker does today and how mature it is, what `nat` needs from it, and the precedents.
